content: 1. When recording event-based dosing in patient records or service registers, it is essential to ensure the confidentiality and security of these records. This is because event-based dosing identifies clients as men who have sex with men (MSM). 2. The recommended reporting period for such data is 12 months. 3. Disaggregation of data should include the following categories: Gender: male, female, transgender. Age groups: 15–19, 20–24, 25–49, and 50+. Experience with PrEP: first-time users and repeat users. Key populations: MSM, people living in prisons or other closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals, adolescent girls, and young women. Dosing type: daily oral PrEP or event-driven PrEP (specific to MSM). 4. A new indicator measures the percentage of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) users who continue oral PrEP for three consecutive months after initiation during the reporting period. This indicator assesses PrEP continuation and loss to follow-up. 5. Studies suggest that many users who discontinue oral PrEP do so within the first few months. This indicator provides insight into early discontinuation rates and the likelihood of continued PrEP use. 6. A low percentage of individuals continuing PrEP at three months should prompt an investigation into the reasons for discontinuation. Programs should be revised accordingly to address these issues. 7. The numerator for this indicator is the number of people who continued PrEP for three consecutive months after initiation during the reporting period. The denominator is the number of people who initiated oral PrEP during the same period. 8. For event-driven dosing among MSM, three-month continuation is defined as reported use of the four-dose regimen around at-risk exposures over a three-month period. Continuation should not be based on the number of pills taken, as this could incorrectly classify clients as non-continuous users. 9. If event-based dosing is recorded, confidentiality and security measures must be in place to protect the identity of MSM clients. 10. The use of antiretroviral medicines by HIV-negative individuals before exposure to HIV can prevent infection. WHO recommends offering oral PrEP containing tenofovir as an additional prevention option for individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection as part of a combination prevention approach. 11. The number of people who received oral PrEP at least once during the reporting period should be counted only once, based on the first time they received PrEP during that period. This includes individuals receiving PrEP through national programs, demonstration projects, research, or private means, provided they follow WHO/UNAIDS standards. 12. Disaggregation for PrEP data should include: Gender: male, female, transgender. Age groups: 15–19, 20–24, 25–49, and 50+. Experience with PrEP: first-time users and repeat users. Key populations: MSM, people in prisons or closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals, adolescent girls, and young women. 13. Knowledge of HIV status is the entry point for people living with HIV to access treatment and care. It also enables those who test HIV-negative to access prevention interventions. 14. The numerator for this indicator is the number of people living with HIV who have received their diagnosis and are still alive. The denominator is the estimated number of people living with HIV. 15. For countries with robust case surveillance and vital registration systems, the number of people who know their HIV status can be derived using tools like the Case Surveillance and Vital Registration (CSAVR) fitting tool in Spectrum AIM. 16. HIV testing volume and positivity rates are critical for monitoring progress toward the UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets. These metrics help assess gaps in testing coverage and better target resources. 17. The percentage of people newly diagnosed with HIV who are initiated on antiretroviral therapy (ART) measures the extent of linkage to care and treatment initiation following diagnosis. Rapid initiation of ART is essential to optimize outcomes and prevent new infections. 18. Disaggregation for ART initiation data should include: Gender: male, female, transgender. Age groups: 0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35–39, 40–44, 45–49, and 50+. Key populations: MSM, people in prisons or closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals. Time to start ART: within 14, 30, or 90 days of diagnosis, as per national guidelines. 19. Index testing and partner notification services measure the coverage and impact of identifying and testing partners and contacts of people living with HIV. This approach has been shown to increase the diagnosis of already-infected contacts and prevent transmission in serodiscordant couples. 20. HIV self-testing (HIVST) is an increasingly common mode of testing that is not captured in other indicators. Monitoring the distribution of HIVST kits provides insight into trends and coverage of this testing approach.
